statement: Five students, including Ana and Ben, stand in a row for a photo. In how many of the possible orders is Ana somewhere to the left of Ben? (They do not have to stand next to each other.)

choices.misconception: I chose the 2 places for Ana and Ben, 10 ways, but forgot that the other three students can stand in different orders.
I only counted orders where Ana stands right next to Ben on his left, treating them as one block: $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$.
I took all 120 orders and removed the 48 orders where Ana and Ben stand next to each other.
I counted all the possible orders of the five students and forgot the condition about Ana and Ben.

hints: First ignore Ana and Ben: how many orders of the five students are there?
Arrangements of a few objects: count all the orders of five students, then use the symmetry between Ana and Ben instead of listing cases.
There are $5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120$ orders. Swapping Ana and Ben turns every order with Ana on the left into one with Ana on the right.

solutions.reliable: Choose the 2 places for Ana and Ben: there are 10 pairs of places, and in each pair Ana must take the left place, so there is only 1 way to put them in. The other three students fill the remaining 3 places in $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ ways. That gives $10 \times 6 = 60$ orders. The transferable idea: place the people with a condition first, then arrange everyone else.
solutions.elegant: All $5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120$ orders split into pairs by swapping Ana and Ben, and in each pair exactly one order has Ana on the left. So the answer is $120 \div 2 = 60$.

whyOnTest: Symmetry halves the count instantly; the traps are forgetting the other students or treating Ana and Ben as a block.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
